title: CLO 2026 Academic Month: The Implementation and Future Possibilities of Digitalization in the International Fashion Market
description: CLO 2026 Official Academic Monthly Course Review Now Available! Vivienne Westwood 3D fashion designer Yao Yao shares experiences in the digital application of the fashion industry, as well as practical performance using CLO.
transcript:
The main topic I want to discuss today is the potential of digital fashion in the international fashion market and some future possibilities.  
Because I have been working overseas, I have a better understanding of the acceptance of digital fashion and cloud software, as well as their practical applications in the actual production process.  

First of all, I will talk about this from the perspective of the more traditional fashion industry, since I also work with a more traditional fashion brand. In fact, digital fashion has started to integrate into the normal workflow of many traditional fashion brands. I will explain this in more detail later.  

Secondly, I will share some case studies. These involve my startup company, ALTA. Our company mainly uses digital fashion, cloud technology, and other digital modeling software to promote digital fashion. We use it to replicate some cultural artifacts or archival fashion—referring to digital clothing based on historical files. Many traditional fashion brands have decades of history and a large number of garments from past fashion shows, which are difficult to preserve. We hope to provide them with a way to unlock the value of this historical culture through digital solutions.  

Finally, I will talk about some relatively new industrial directions, such as digital fashion. In fact, there are many new developments under this broad fashion lens—for example, some fashion weeks dedicated to digital fashion, digital fashion shows, digital fashion films, and so on. There are also concepts related to the metaverse that became popular a few years ago. I will share a few cases on this as well. The last part will be a Q&A session, and I look forward to the opportunity to communicate with you.  

Let's begin with the digital upgrade of the traditional fashion industry. I will focus on two aspects. The first is the actual digital upgrade in our production process. The second is how we use CGI to assist sales or social media operations.  

This is a general overview of how the production process works in traditional fashion companies. Since I believe many of my peers may also be learning design themselves, I won’t go into too much detail. This is a very large topic.  

Generally, we start with a design idea, then find the right fabric, and produce a tech pack that matches the supplier or factory. This is the technical package. Then we create the traditional pattern. During the pattern-making process, you find that from the visual design to the final pattern, a lot of trial and error is required.  

During sample production, it usually takes three to five samples to achieve the final result and produce a perfect sample.  

Now, some traditional fashion brands have started to use 3D modeling. For example, at the fitting stage, many brands have begun to use digital fitting. Of course, this is not yet universal, and not all products use digital fitting completely. When I worked at Vivienne Westwood, we had many fittings done through traditional methods, which is why many of our garments show creases or asymmetrical structures.  

A large part of the pattern is transformed into a digital pattern after fitting, then imported into CLO for adjustment and upgrades until the final production stage. This process saves us a lot of time and fabric costs. Through 3D visual support, we can achieve perfect production effects quickly.  

Starting from a production perspective, here is another example from a British lingerie brand I worked with on a collaborative project. They use 3D visualization to assist with fabric selection. You can see the three-dimensional rendering on the right side.  

I will reveal the answer here: all of these are renderings, including very detailed laser effects and small fabric buttons on the lingerie—all completed in CLO through modeling and rendering.  

This brand uses many of these rendered images directly on their own e-commerce platform as product pictures to help users better understand the style.  

Here is a short video clip. On the left, you can see the front and back views as separate rendered images. This is done by adding a flat panel during rendering. This method is very helpful, especially for laser effects, which create a translucent look. When viewing the lingerie from the front, the structure behind it does not interfere. Even for complex laser effects, you don’t need to see the back from the front view.  

Another feature is coloring. CLO allows multiple colors in the same file, which is a very good example. We can use the same product file to develop different color versions.  

Next, let’s move to the second part, about my startup company and how we use digital fashion to unlock historical cultural value.  

First, some background: anyone who studies fashion or art understands that much innovation is based on history. Many designers draw inspiration from history for their current research. Looking back, besides the modern fashion industry established after the Industrial Revolution, every era from ancient Egypt, ancient China, India, and others had its own form of fashion. At that time, it was not called a fashion industry but reflected national customs, fabric research, shrinkage techniques, or other crafts.  

In modern fashion design, we gather a lot of inspiration from the world’s history. This foundation is built on history, especially for many luxury brands with rich historical heritage. However, unlocking the value of this heritage is often very difficult.  

Why do I say that? Here is a case study: Mugler, a very traditional French high-end fashion brand, held an exhibition in the United States in 2025 (if I remember correctly). Over the past 50 years, Mugler has designed more than 10 million pieces of clothing. But in their archive or database, the preserved amount is very small—they cannot store more than 10,000 sets of clothing due to space constraints.  

The exhibition they held in the past two years was the largest in recent years, displaying 150 pieces of clothing for seven months. Compared to the 50 years and 10,000 sets in their history, this exhibition showed only a very small fragment of the archive.  

So, we have been thinking about how to help these traditional brands better protect and inherit historical garments. I believe we are entering a new era where we can use the rich historical value of brands together with today’s digital audience to create deeper interaction.  

Nowadays, more and more information is online. For example, this exhibition was in New York—I might not be able to buy a ticket or be there during those seven months. But if there is a corresponding online or digital exhibition, I believe everyone would be willing to click on the link to explore and learn.  

Here is a case study illustrating how we use digital methods to unlock infinite future possibilities based on the past.  

You can see this rotating small model. This is a digital restoration of Mugler’s Parker Ray Band from the 1970s. It is a typical piece digitally modeled by us.  

Another example is a phoenix from Chinese history, a symbol many are familiar with. This phoenix style, or similar types, can be seen in museums, crafted with a specific technique that today is impossible to reproduce because it requires three-dimensional craftsmanship in space.  

Our digital disassembly of the phoenix allows audiences and customers to understand this craftsmanship, which otherwise cannot be comprehended. This is part of our social contribution.  

You can also see horse-riding images or historical patterns. These are from horse-riding outfits of the time. The shape of the skirt is designed for convenience—when riding a horse, a buckle at the waist fixes the skirt to the body for ease of movement.  

In this section, we received historical documents from the French Academy, including photos of costumes from different angles. However, digitization faces great difficulty because most historical costumes lack pattern documents from the time. These pattern documents are hard to preserve, especially if they include three-dimensional decals or specific craftsmanship, or if the paper versions are fragile.  

This is why we collaborate with various market brands, universities, and museums. It is a big challenge. We often need to re-digitize all existing data and bring these patterns back to the present.  

This is a specific exhibition page we created, where you can enter the historical story introduction through an interactive interface. You can scroll down to see the historical pages, actually experiencing what you would see during the exhibition. There is even a modern innovation where you can scan a QR code to open a visual effect on the website.  

Six years ago, I discussed how to unlock some of these historical values. Now, I will introduce some new directions in our industry, which may be more interesting.  

First, I want to introduce a project I completed last year in collaboration with the Roblox platform. The process for this project used CLO for 3D modeling. In the normal design process, we complete all details, including name design, materials on the clothes, and small pattern designs. After finishing, we use CLO’s UV generation function to guide the model, export it to other software to create a simplified model, and make it compatible with Roblox’s platform standards.  

For background, Roblox is very popular especially in the United States and Europe as a virtual world platform where many people socialize and make friends. It is especially popular among young generations—kids around 10 years old or younger, and teenagers around 16 years old.  

I once collaborated with a friend on this topic, whose son is about 10 years old. The son told me that at school, whenever he meets a new friend, the first question is whether they have a Roblox account, and they almost always add each other. It’s similar to how we used to add each other on QQ when we were in elementary school.  

The difference with Roblox is that users can publish their own design series and even sell their own digital clothes.  

This is a concept image from the series I designed called “Defensive Battle.” The concept combines armor design with cold ice-like shapes reminiscent of weapons from a certain era, blended with flame restoration elements. There are three sets of clothes in total.  

The three images you see are the results of my production and rendering in CLO. We last brought this product to the Roblox platform, where various styles are available.  

This small model shows different square-shaped robot-like figures, and you can customize some styles. In tests, we tried putting the costume on different models to observe effects with different poses and movements.  

You can also design different color versions, as shown in the first video, with yellow, blue, pink, and other new versions.  

This is another platform, a cross-border collaboration in the metaverse called “Digital Misculture,” which represents modern culture encountered in digital fashion.  

We held an open call to collect 10 artists from around the world, working with them to digitize their local cultural costumes and bring them into the digital world. This was a collaboration with the metaverse platform, releasing an online event featuring runway shows and interactions.  

Here you can clearly see a lookbook of the ten costumes displayed together, representing various countries. The first is obviously from China, the second from Nigeria (notable for its beadwork on the head), followed by Indian and Japanese clothing. We also showed a French-made garment previously mentioned.  

All these different styles were created through one-on-one collaborations with artists or with the Academy of Fine Arts.  

This is a gallery where you can see all the clothes, made in CLO with dye effects.  

This is an introduction to the exhibition on the Decentraland platform, where we have our own exhibition hall. You can see a triangular outdoor pavilion that you can enter to explore the metaverse exhibition.  

Behind it is a large screen playing a concept-based walkthrough video. You can also view static exhibits and relevant information inside the hall.  

This platform allows you to walk around the metaverse, buy virtual land, interact, chat, and more.  

At the same time, as this was part of Decentraland Fashion Week, many other brands also had exhibition spaces on the platform.  

This is another view of the Decentraland exhibition hall. On this platform, you can digitize your own style and wear digital clothes. This is different from the previous static exhibition, as it is more interactive—you can wear the clothes on your avatar, do DIY styling in the exhibition hall, and view the results.  

Here is another exhibition hall with a map introduction. After entering, you can see the layout with spaces for panel talks, posters on walls, and live broadcasts or online sharing sessions.  

This is our small exhibition area, showing the same costume series but in a different way. You can dance or communicate with others.  

The costumes are not as perfect as before, and there are some variations on avatars’ bodies, which I think is a limitation of current digital technology.  

Of course, this interface also supports real-time communication. It is becoming more accurate and effective, but it still requires time to improve.  

This project is from about three years ago. I will now share a video I made (muted for your convenience). It was released during Digital Fashion Week and is inspired by Alexander McQueen.  

He once held a fashion show featuring a model with fireworks and self-destruction scenes, honoring Saint-Eugène, a French female warrior.  

To honor him, I created a series inspired by history, with two corresponding chapters in the video.  

We are now looking at the first chapter, a reenactment honoring Saint-Eugène, who died on the battlefield, falling into the fire. These scenes were digitally created in CLO and animated in Unreal Engine.  

The second chapter represents a modern homage and uses this concept to design a whole series of clothes and a digital show. It represents the history of destruction and the rebirth of modern concepts.  

All costumes were sculpted in CLO, showing delicate details. Of course, looking at the model now, it feels a bit fake and amusing, but time was limited, so we tried our best within a short period.  

This is a dress with a fire-burning concept. The original video had exciting background music.  

Finally, this is the ending pose of the series.  

This concludes all my sharing today. I am very happy to have this opportunity to communicate with everyone.  

Hello. Hello. Hello. Hello. Hello. Hello. Hello. Hello. Hello. Hello. Hello. Hello.

chunks.content: # The Implementation and Future Possibilities of Digitalization in the International Fashion Market This document explores the integration of digital fashion and cloud software into traditional fashion workflows, the use of digital technology to preserve historical fashion heritage, and innovative applications of digital fashion in virtual platforms and the metaverse. Key terms include digital fashion, 3D modeling, CLO software, digital heritage preservation, Roblox, Decentraland, and metaverse fashion exhibitions. --- ## Digital Upgrades in Traditional Fashion Industry Workflows This section covers how digital technology, especially 3D modeling and cloud software like CLO, is transforming traditional fashion production and sales processes. Traditional fashion production begins with design concepts, fabric sourcing, and the creation of a tech pack for suppliers or factories. Pattern-making involves significant trial and error, often requiring three to five sample iterations to finalize a garment. Increasingly, brands are incorporating 3D digital fitting into the production process. While not yet universal, digital fitting reduces physical samples, saving time and fabric costs. For example, at Vivienne Westwood, traditional fittings resulted in garments with creases or asymmetrical structures, highlighting the limitations of non-digital processes. A significant portion of patterns is converted into digital formats and imported into CLO for refinement before final production. CLO enables quick adjustments and visualization, improving accuracy and reducing waste. **Case Study: British Lingerie Brand** - Utilizes 3D visualization to assist fabric selection. - CLO software produces detailed renderings, including laser effects and small fabric buttons. - Rendered images serve as product pictures on e-commerce platforms, enhancing customer understanding. - CLO supports multi-color variants within a single file, enabling efficient development of color versions. --- ## Using Digital Fashion to Unlock Historical Cultural Value This section focuses on using digital fashion technology to preserve, restore, and exhibit historical garments and cultural artifacts, especially for luxury brands with extensive archives. Historical fashion inspiration spans from ancient civilizations (Egypt, China, India) to modern fashion post-Industrial Revolution. Many luxury brands have rich archives but face challenges preserving physical garments due to space and fragility. **Case Study: Mugler Archive and Exhibition** - Mugler, a French high-end fashion brand, has designed over 10 million garments over 50 years. - Archive physically stores fewer than 10,000 garments due to space limitations. - A 2025 US exhibition displayed 150 pieces over seven months, representing a small fraction of Mugler's history. - Digital solutions can unlock broader access and engagement with heritage garments beyond physical exhibitions. **Digital Restoration Examples** - Digital model of Mugler’s 1970s Parker Ray Band created for online interaction. - Chinese phoenix motif restored digitally to reveal complex three-dimensional craftsmanship otherwise impossible to reproduce physically. - Digitized horse-riding outfits with functional skirt designs fixed by waist buckles for riding convenience. Historical garments often lack surviving pattern documents, especially for 3D embellishments or fragile paper patterns. Collaboration with brands, universities, and museums is essential to re-digitize and reconstruct these archives. **Digital Exhibition Interface** - Interactive webpages simulate historical exhibition experiences. - QR codes link to enhanced visual effects online.

chunks.title: CLO 2026 Academic Month: The Implementation and Future Possibilities of Digitalization in the International Fashion Market
chunks.content: - Chinese phoenix motif restored digitally to reveal complex three-dimensional craftsmanship otherwise impossible to reproduce physically. - Digitized horse-riding outfits with functional skirt designs fixed by waist buckles for riding convenience. Historical garments often lack surviving pattern documents, especially for 3D embellishments or fragile paper patterns. Collaboration with brands, universities, and museums is essential to re-digitize and reconstruct these archives. **Digital Exhibition Interface** - Interactive webpages simulate historical exhibition experiences. - QR codes link to enhanced visual effects online. - These platforms expand access to cultural heritage for global digital audiences. --- ## Innovative Digital Fashion Applications and Metaverse Collaborations This section highlights recent projects combining digital fashion design with virtual platforms and metaverse environments, demonstrating new possibilities for fashion experiences and commerce. ### CLO and Roblox Collaboration - CLO used for detailed 3D modeling, including textures, materials, and patterns. - UV mapping guides model export to simplified formats compatible with Roblox. - Roblox is popular among children and teenagers in the US and Europe as a social virtual world. - Users create, share, and sell digital clothing within the platform. **Project: “Defensive Battle” Series** - Armor-inspired digital clothing with cold ice and flame motifs. - Three distinct outfits rendered in CLO and imported to Roblox. - Customizable square-shaped robot avatars wear these outfits with varied poses and movements. - Multiple color variants designed and tested. ### “Digital Misculture” Metaverse Project - Collaborative initiative with 10 international artists digitizing local cultural costumes. - Hosted digital runway shows and interactive online events. - Costumes represent diverse cultures including Chinese, Nigerian (noted for beadwork), Indian, Japanese, and French designs. - Created with one-on-one artist collaborations and partnerships with the Academy of Fine Arts. - CLO used for detailed dye effect simulations. ### Decentraland Fashion Week Exhibition - Digital exhibition hall featuring a triangular outdoor pavilion. - Large screen plays concept walkthrough videos. - Visitors can explore static exhibits, view information, and interact in real time. - Platform supports buying virtual land, chatting, and socializing. - Exhibition areas include panel talks, posters, live broadcasts, and online sharing. - Avatars can wear digital clothes, customize styles, and dance or communicate. - Current digital clothing has limitations with avatar body variations and realism. - Real-time communication features are improving but still evolving. --- ## Digital Fashion Storytelling and Animation This section presents a creative project combining historical inspiration with digital animation and garment design. **Alexander McQueen Inspired Series** - Tribute to Saint-Eugène, a French female warrior. - Two-part video: first chapter reenacts the battlefield death and fire; second chapter presents a modern rebirth concept. - Costumes digitally sculpted in CLO showing intricate detail. - Animation created using Unreal Engine. - Dresses include a fire-burning theme. - Time constraints limited realism, but the series demonstrates potential for digital storytelling in fashion. --- # Summary Digital fashion is increasingly integrated with traditional fashion workflows through 3D modeling and cloud software, enhancing production efficiency and marketing.

Digital technology enables preservation and interactive exhibition of historical fashion heritage, overcoming physical archive limitations. Emerging collaborations with virtual platforms like Roblox and Decentraland demonstrate novel ways to design, showcase, and commercialize digital garments, engaging younger audiences and expanding the cultural reach of fashion.
